title: The Second Machine Age: Work, Progress, and Prosperity in a Time of Brilliant Technologies
source_note: Book text not read; facts come from the Wikipedia article, a strategy+business piece on the book and a PopMatters review. Freestyle chess is Kasparov's own 2005 account (via secondary reports), not confirmed as a passage of the book.

facts.claim: The Second Machine Age (W. W. Norton, 2014) is by Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee and continues their earlier Race Against the Machine.

The first machine age (Industrial Revolution) had machines automate or augment physical tasks; the second does the same for cognitive tasks. The authors advise people to 'race with the machine, not against it', aiming for machines that complement humans rather than substitute for them.
Examples in the book: software that grades essays more objectively, consistently and quickly than humans, and Forbes.com corporate-earnings previews generated by algorithms without human involvement.

Chessboard story: an inventor asks for one grain of rice on the first of 64 squares, two on the next, and so on, doubling each time. By the 32nd square the total is about 4 billion grains, roughly one large rice field's yield; by the 64th it is more than 18 quintillion grains, a pile taller than Mount Everest. Some versions say the emperor had the inventor executed. Ray Kurzweil popularised the idea of the 'second half of the chessboard' in 1999.

The authors take 1958, when the first silicon transistors were commercialised, as the start of the doubling and argue digital technology has entered the second half of the chessboard, where numbers outstrip our ability to comprehend them. Our brains are not equipped to grasp sustained exponential growth.
Moore's Law: Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that transistor counts doubled on a regular schedule, later put at about every two years. It is an observation, not a physical law.

A 1982 Osborne Executive was 500 times larger, 100 times heavier, ten times more expensive and 1/100 as fast as a 2007 iPhone. The 2011 iPad 2 matched the processor speed of the 1985 Cray-2, which cost an inflation-adjusted $33 million.

Driverless car: in 2002 DARPA offered US$1 million for a race over a 150-mile Mojave Desert course. In the 2004 race no entrant finished; the farthest went 7.4 miles. Less than six years later Google's autonomous car had logged hundreds of thousands of accident-free miles.

Kasparov's account (NYRB 2010) of a 2005 Playchess.com freestyle tournament: the winners were two amateur Americans using three computers at once. His formula: a weak human plus machine plus a better process beat a strong computer alone and a strong human plus machine plus an inferior process. A separate report names the team ZackS and a 2.5-1.5 win over a 14-year-old Russian grandmaster in the final.
facts.source: search result quoting Kasparov; not confirmed in the book

facts.claim: Kodak employed over 145,000 people directly, a third of them at its Rochester, New York headquarters; Instagram, built on digital photo data, had 15 employees.

Bounty is the growing number, diversity and quality of goods available at falling prices, and the authors say GDP is inadequate for measuring it. Spread is growing differences in wealth, income and mobility between people; drivers named: skill-biased technical change, capital income rising relative to labour income, and superstar effects. The authors argue for maximising bounty while limiting spread.
Digital goods can be copied at close to zero cost, perfectly and instantly (non-rival).
facts.source: author's knowledge of the book's digital-goods argument; not confirmed in fetched pages

facts.claim: Computer-chess expert Kenneth Regan's data (as cited by a blog post) shows a striking share of the most accurate games ever played came from human-computer teams; the post also lists how humans add value (pruning variations, spotting where programs disagree, managing time) and warns humans may soon add nothing, as in checkers.
